title: Demonstrate an understand of the basic structure of ornamental plants

lessons.title: Roots, stems and leaves
lessons.html:
Roots, stems and leaves

Every plant has parts. Each part has a job. When you know the parts, you know how to look after the plant and you can see when something is wrong.

Roots

Roots grow under the ground. Their jobs are:

  • To hold the plant in the soil so it does not fall over.
  • To take up water and plant food from the soil.
  • In some plants, to store food. For example, a carrot or a dahlia tuber.

The thin, fine roots at the ends do most of the work of taking up water. They break easily. That is why we handle root balls gently when we plant.

Stems

The stem holds the plant up. It carries water from the roots up to the leaves. It also carries food made in the leaves down to the roots and other parts.

  • Soft stems: in annuals like petunias.
  • Woody stems: in shrubs and trees. A tree's thick stem is the trunk.

On the stem there are nodes, where leaves and buds grow. A bud is a small bump that can grow into a new shoot or a flower. When we prune, we cut just above a bud.

Leaves

Leaves are the food factory of the plant. They use sunlight, air and water to make food. This is called photosynthesis. Leaves are green because of a green material called chlorophyll.

Leaves also let water out through tiny holes, mostly underneath. On a hot day a plant loses a lot of water through its leaves. That is why plants wilt when it is hot and dry.

Leaves come in many shapes: long and thin like grass, round, divided like a fern, or thick and fleshy like an aloe.

lessons.title: Flowers, fruit and seeds
lessons.html:
Flowers, fruit and seeds

Many ornamental plants are grown for their flowers. But for the plant, flowers have an important job: to make seeds, so new plants can grow.

Parts of a flower

PartJob
PetalsBright colours and smell bring bees, birds and butterflies
SepalsSmall green leaves that protect the flower bud
Stamens (male)Make yellow powder called pollen
Pistil (female)Receives pollen and makes seeds inside

From flower to seed

  1. A bee or bird visits the flower and carries pollen from one flower to another. This is called pollination.
  2. The pollen fertilises the flower.
  3. The petals fall off.
  4. A fruit grows. Inside the fruit are seeds.
  5. The seeds can grow into new plants.

Sunbirds pollinate strelitzias, aloes and wild dagga. Bees pollinate many flowers. This is one reason we must be careful with chemicals: they can kill bees.

Deadheading

On many flowering plants, we cut off old dead flowers. This is called deadheading. The plant then does not use its energy to make seeds, and it makes more flowers instead.

Why this matters at work

  • Damaged roots mean the plant cannot drink. Handle roots gently.
  • Broken stems stop water from reaching the leaves.
  • Leaves need light. Plants in deep shade grow thin and weak.
  • Without bees and birds, many plants make no seed.

Key points

  • Roots hold the plant and take up water and food.
  • Stems hold the plant up and carry water and food.
  • Leaves make food from sunlight (photosynthesis) and lose water.
  • Flowers make seeds after pollination.
  • Deadheading old flowers gives more new flowers.
